Short PSKs are vulnerable to offline dictionary and brute-force attacks against captured IKE aggressive mode or main mode handshakes. IKE aggressive mode in particular exposes the PSK hash to passive capture, enabling offline cracking with tools like hashcat. Industry standards (NIST SP 800-77, RFC 4306) recommend PSKs of at least 20 characters with high entropy. PSKs under 8 characters can be cracked in seconds with GPU acceleration.

how_to_obtain.instruction: On Cisco IOS/IOS-XE, extract all IKEv1 and IKEv2 pre-shared key values and measure the length of the shortest one.
how_to_obtain.command: show running-config | include ^crypto isakmp key|pre-shared-key | awk '{for(i=1;i<=NF;i++) if(length($i)>4 && $i~/[a-zA-Z0-9!@#$%^&*]/) print length($i), $i}' | sort -n | head -5
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Length values in ascending order; first line shows the shortest PSK length. Values below 20 indicate psk_minimum_length < 20 and trigger the policy.

how_to_obtain.instruction: On StrongSwan/OpenSwan, read PSK values from ipsec.secrets and calculate the minimum length across all entries.
how_to_obtain.command: grep -v '^#\|^$' /etc/ipsec.secrets | grep -oP '(?<=")[^"]+(?=")|(?<=: PSK )\S+' | awk '{print length($0), $0}' | sort -n | head -3
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Length and PSK value per line sorted ascending; minimum length value should be >= 20 for compliant configuration.

how_to_obtain.instruction: On Palo Alto Networks GlobalProtect or IPsec tunnel configuration, retrieve pre-shared key lengths via the CLI (keys are masked but length may be retrievable via API or config export).
how_to_obtain.command: show config running | xpath /config/devices/entry/network/ike/gateway | match pre-shared-key
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Masked key entries; use API config export with admin credentials for plaintext review, then count character length of each PSK value.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Request the VPN configuration baseline or provisioning template from the network operations team to verify whether a minimum PSK length standard is enforced at the time of tunnel creation.
how_to_obtain.navigation: Review VPN provisioning standards documentation, configuration templates, or automation scripts that generate PSK values. Verify use of a random key generator with minimum 20-character output.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Provisioning script or template demonstrating PSK generation with minimum 20 characters of random alphanumeric and special characters; alternatively, extract and measure current PSK lengths from device configs.

typical_values: 8-12 (common in legacy deployments using human-memorable passwords)
16 (partially compliant, below the 20-character best practice threshold)
20-32 (compliant with NIST and industry best practice recommendations)
0 (indicates PSK not configured or unable to retrieve)

option_description: Controls whether the VPN gateway captures and forwards authentication-related events including failed login attempts, successful authentications, session initiations, and session disconnects. These events are essential for detecting brute-force attacks, credential stuffing campaigns, and unauthorized access patterns.
security_impact: The Rego policy fires 'insufficient_authentication_logging' when auth_event_logging_enabled is false, and additionally when logging is enabled but required fields (timestamp, source_ip, username) are missing from log records, or when log retention is under 30 days. Without authentication logging, T1110 (Brute Force) and T1110.004 (Credential Stuffing) attacks proceed undetected, and post-incident forensic reconstruction is impossible. Regulatory frameworks including PCI-DSS Requirement 10.2 and NIST 800-53 AU-2 mandate logging of authentication events. This is a foundational detective control that enables SIEM correlation rules to alert on anomalous authentication patterns.

how_to_obtain.instruction: On Cisco ASA, verify that logging is enabled, authentication events are included, and a syslog server is configured for remote log forwarding.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: 'logging enable', 'logging host <syslog-server-ip>', 'logging trap informational' or higher severity, and 'aaa accounting' entries confirm auth event logging is active. Absence of these lines means auth_event_logging_enabled: false.

how_to_obtain.instruction: On a Linux-based VPN gateway (OpenVPN, StrongSwan), verify that authentication events are captured in syslog or a dedicated log file and forwarded to a central SIEM.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Recent log entries showing authentication success/failure events with timestamps, usernames, and source IPs. Empty output or no log file indicates auth_event_logging_enabled: false.

how_to_obtain.instruction: On Fortinet FortiGate, verify that VPN authentication events are logged to FortiLog or a remote syslog server with appropriate log severity.
how_to_obtain.navigation: Log & Report > Log Settings: verify 'VPN Activity' and 'Authentication Events' are enabled; Log & Report > Remote Logging: confirm syslog server IP is configured with severity 'Information' or lower.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: VPN Activity logging checkbox enabled with remote syslog server configured; test log connectivity confirms events are being forwarded.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Query the SIEM or log aggregation system to verify that VPN authentication events are arriving from the gateway in real time, with required fields present.
how_to_obtain.command: grep -E '(failed|accepted|rejected|authenticated|disconnect)' /var/log/vpn/auth.log | head -20 | awk '{print NF, $0}' | sort -rn | head -5
how_to_obtain.navigation: In SIEM (Splunk/ELK/Sentinel): search for source=<vpn-gateway-ip> (authentication OR login OR disconnect) | table _time, src_ip, user, action | limit 20
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Log events containing timestamp, source IP, username, and action (success/failure) fields confirm auth_event_logging_enabled: true with required fields. Gap in recent events or missing fields indicates misconfiguration.

typical_values: false (common in SMB environments, legacy appliances, or when default logging configuration is not modified)
true (enterprise environments with SIEM integration and compliance requirements)

option_description: Controls which data fields are captured per authentication event in VPN gateway logs, including timestamp, source_ip, username, device_id, session_id, and event_type. Determines the forensic completeness of the authentication audit trail.
security_impact: The Rego policy triggers the 'insufficient_authentication_logging' finding when 'timestamp', 'source_ip', or 'username' are absent from logged_auth_fields. Missing fields directly impair detection of brute-force and credential-stuffing campaigns (T1110, T1110.004) because analysts cannot correlate attack patterns without source IP or identify targeted accounts without username. Incomplete logs also prevent retrospective investigation of compromised sessions.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Pull a sample of recent authentication log entries from the VPN syslog stream or local log file and identify which fields are consistently present across success, failure, and disconnect events.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Each log line should contain a timestamp, source IP address, username, device identifier or hostname, session ID, and event classification (success/failure/disconnect).

how_to_obtain.instruction: For Cisco ASA/FTD: navigate to Monitoring > Logging > Real-Time Log Viewer and filter on authentication syslog message IDs (713228, 722051, 722037). For Palo Alto GlobalProtect: navigate to Monitor > Logs > GlobalProtect and inspect the column set. For Fortinet FortiGate: navigate to Log & Report > VPN Events and review displayed fields.
how_to_obtain.navigation: Cisco ASA: Monitoring > Logging > Real-Time Log Viewer | Palo Alto: Monitor > Logs > GlobalProtect | FortiGate: Log & Report > VPN Events
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Log entries display all six expected fields: timestamp, source IP, username, device ID, session ID, and event type.

how_to_obtain.instruction: For Palo Alto GlobalProtect, query the operational CLI for recent HIP and authentication logs to enumerate captured fields.
how_to_obtain.command: show log globalprotect direction equal backward | match 'srcip\|user\|sessionid\|eventid'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Output rows include srcip, user, sessionid, and eventid columns confirming all required fields are logged.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Query a SIEM or syslog aggregator (e.g., Splunk, Elastic) for recent VPN authentication events and inspect field coverage programmatically.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: JSON response contains all six field names populated in at least 95% of returned records.

option_description: Specifies the number of days that authentication log data is retained on the VPN gateway or a connected log management system. Determines how far back analysts can investigate historical authentication events.
security_impact: The Rego policy triggers 'insufficient_authentication_logging' when log_retention_days is less than 30. Short retention windows prevent retrospective investigation of slow-burn brute-force campaigns (T1110) and credential-stuffing attacks (T1110.004) that may not be detected in real time. Regulators and frameworks such as PCI DSS and NIST 800-53 mandate minimum 90-day online and 12-month total retention for access logs.

how_to_obtain.instruction: For Cisco ASA: navigate to Configuration > Device Management > Logging > Logging Setup and review the 'Log Buffer Size' and any configured log server retention policies. For FortiGate: navigate to Log & Report > Log Settings and inspect local disk or remote syslog retention. For Palo Alto: navigate to Device > Log Settings and check the retention period configured per log type.
how_to_obtain.navigation: Cisco ASA: Configuration > Device Management > Logging > Logging Setup | FortiGate: Log & Report > Log Settings | Palo Alto: Device > Log Settings
how_to_obtain.expected_output: A numeric retention value of 90 days or greater is configured for authentication-related log categories.

how_to_obtain.instruction: On Linux-based VPN appliances (OpenVPN, strongSwan), inspect logrotate configuration to determine how many rotated log files are retained and calculate total retention days.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Rotate count multiplied by rotation interval should equal at least 90 days (e.g., 'daily' with 'rotate 90' or 'weekly' with 'rotate 13').

how_to_obtain.instruction: Query the SIEM or syslog platform API to determine the oldest authentication log record timestamp, which reveals the effective retention window.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: The timestamp on the oldest returned record should be at least 90 days prior to the current date.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Interview the VPN or SOC team to determine whether a SIEM, syslog server, or cloud log archive stores VPN authentication events separately from local appliance storage, and confirm the configured retention policy in that system.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Documented retention policy specifying a minimum of 90 days online retention for VPN authentication events, with written evidence of enforcement.

option_description: Controls whether the VPN gateway enforces a device health and posture assessment—verifying OS patch level, EDR agent presence, and disk encryption state—as a prerequisite before granting tunnel access to any connecting client.
security_impact: The Rego policy triggers 'no_client_endpoint_posture_check' when endpoint_posture_check_enabled is false or not set. Without posture gating, unmanaged, unpatched, or malware-infected endpoints can authenticate and gain full tunnel access, enabling external remote service abuse (T1133) and introduction of unauthorized remote access tools (T1219) into the corporate network. This is the primary gate preventing BYOD and compromised contractor machines from tunneling into internal resources.

how_to_obtain.instruction: For Cisco AnyConnect/ASA: navigate to Configuration > Remote Access VPN > Network (Client) Access > Group Policies, select a policy, and check whether 'HostScan' or 'DAP (Dynamic Access Policy)' with posture conditions is enabled. For Palo Alto GlobalProtect: navigate to Network > GlobalProtect > Gateways, select a gateway, and review HIP Profile bindings under the Security Policies tab. For Fortinet: navigate to VPN > SSL-VPN Settings and check endpoint compliance profile assignment.
how_to_obtain.navigation: Cisco ASA: Configuration > Remote Access VPN > Network (Client) Access > Group Policies | Palo Alto: Network > GlobalProtect > Gateways | FortiGate: VPN > SSL-VPN Settings
how_to_obtain.expected_output: A posture/HIP/HostScan policy is referenced and set to 'enforce' or 'required' rather than 'optional' or 'disabled'.

how_to_obtain.instruction: On Cisco ASA, display the running configuration to identify HostScan image and DAP policy assignments.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Output includes 'csd hostscan image' and 'dap' entries referencing an active posture policy bound to tunnel groups.

how_to_obtain.instruction: On Palo Alto, query the operational CLI to list configured HIP objects and profiles, confirming at least one is active.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Output lists at least one HIP profile with match criteria defined, indicating posture enforcement is configured.

how_to_obtain.instruction: For FortiGate SSL-VPN, review the exported configuration file for the endpoint-compliance reference within the SSL-VPN realms or portals.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Configuration block shows 'set endpoint-compliance enable' or a reference to an endpoint compliance profile within the VPN portal definition.

option_description: Defines the breadth of posture check enforcement across VPN connection profiles or tunnel groups. 'all' means every connection profile enforces posture; 'partial' means only selected profiles do; 'none' means no profiles enforce posture regardless of whether the feature is enabled.
security_impact: The Rego policy triggers 'no_client_endpoint_posture_check' when posture_enforcement_scope is 'partial', even if endpoint_posture_check_enabled is true. Profiles lacking posture enforcement become unguarded entry points where unmanaged or compromised endpoints connect freely, defeating the overall posture control. Attackers specifically probe for guest tunnel groups or fallback profiles (T1133) that bypass enforcement.

how_to_obtain.instruction: On Cisco ASA, enumerate all tunnel-group configurations and check whether each references a DAP policy or HostScan-enforcing group policy.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Every tunnel-group entry references a group-policy that has HostScan/DAP posture enforcement; any profile referencing a policy without posture indicates 'partial' scope.

how_to_obtain.instruction: For Palo Alto GlobalProtect: navigate to Policies > Security and filter on GlobalProtect zones; for each rule, verify that a HIP Profile match condition is present. Navigate to Network > GlobalProtect > Gateways and confirm that all gateway configurations reference the HIP profile in their security policy. Profiles without a HIP condition are unprotected.
how_to_obtain.navigation: Palo Alto: Policies > Security (filter by GlobalProtect zone) | Network > GlobalProtect > Gateways
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Every security policy associated with GlobalProtect traffic includes a HIP Profile match condition; absence in any rule indicates 'partial' scope.

how_to_obtain.instruction: For FortiGate, list all SSL-VPN portals and check each for endpoint compliance configuration.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Each portal block contains 'set endpoint-compliance enable'; any portal block lacking this line indicates 'partial' or 'none' scope.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Request the VPN administrator to provide a complete list of all tunnel groups, connection profiles, and portals with their associated posture enforcement status. Cross-reference against the list of groups actively assigned to users in the directory.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: A matrix showing every connection profile and its posture enforcement status; all profiles should be marked as enforced for a result of 'all'.

option_description: Indicates whether the VPN gateway explicitly permits connections from devices not enrolled in or recognized by the organization's MDM or UEM platform, even when posture checking is nominally configured. Includes bypass rules, guest tunnel groups, or fallback profiles that skip device enrollment verification.
security_impact: The Rego policy triggers 'no_client_endpoint_posture_check' when unmanaged_device_access_allowed is true, even when endpoint_posture_check_enabled is also true. Allowing unmanaged devices creates a posture bypass path where personal, contractor, or attacker-controlled endpoints connect without certificate-based device authentication or MDM enrollment verification (T1133, T1219). This nullifies the posture investment for all scenarios where an attacker can present as an unmanaged device.

how_to_obtain.instruction: For Cisco ASA with AnyConnect: navigate to Configuration > Remote Access VPN > Dynamic Access Policies and review DAP rules. Check for any rule with a 'NoMatch' or catch-all condition that grants 'continue' access without requiring an MDM or certificate-based device check. For Palo Alto GlobalProtect: navigate to Network > GlobalProtect > Gateways and check whether any security policy allows access when the HIP profile match fails (i.e., a default-allow rule exists for non-HIP-matched traffic).
how_to_obtain.navigation: Cisco ASA: Configuration > Remote Access VPN > Dynamic Access Policies | Palo Alto: Network > GlobalProtect > Gateways > Security Policy (check deny-on-HIP-mismatch)
how_to_obtain.expected_output: No DAP rule or gateway security policy permits tunnel establishment for devices failing MDM enrollment or certificate checks; any such permissive fallback rule indicates unmanaged access is allowed.

how_to_obtain.instruction: On Cisco ASA, check DAP configuration for permissive fallback actions that would allow unmanaged devices.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: No DAP record with 'action = continue' exists without a corresponding MDM or HostScan attribute match; a 'terminate' action on the catch-all record indicates unmanaged devices are blocked.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Inspect VPN gateway configuration for guest tunnel group definitions or fallback profile entries that omit certificate authentication requirements.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: No configuration blocks allowing connections without certificate-based device authentication; absence of these keywords in non-commented lines indicates unmanaged access is not configured.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Interview the VPN administrator and request documentation of any formally approved exceptions or guest access profiles that bypass MDM enrollment requirements, including their justification and expiration dates.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Either no documented exceptions exist (confirming unmanaged_device_access_allowed = false) or exceptions are documented with a compensating control plan.

option_description: Identifies the OS privilege level of the account under which the VPN service process executes. Categories are: root_or_system (maximum OS privilege), domain_admin (full AD domain control), local_admin (local machine administrative rights), or least_privilege (dedicated low-privilege service account).
security_impact: The Rego policy triggers 'privileged_account_used_for_vpn_service_identity' for root_or_system and domain_admin unconditionally, and for local_admin when the account is also shared. VPN services are exposed to the internet and have historically been targeted for pre-auth RCE. If the service process runs as root or SYSTEM, a successful exploit immediately yields full OS control (T1548.002) and enables privileged service execution (T1569.002). Domain admin level provides AD-wide lateral movement with no further escalation required.

how_to_obtain.instruction: On Linux, identify the process owner of the VPN daemon (OpenVPN, strongSwan charon, ocserv) using ps.
how_to_obtain.command: ps aux | grep -E 'openvpn|charon|ocserv|vpnd|ipsec' | grep -v grep | awk '{print $1}'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Process owner should be a dedicated non-root service account such as 'openvpn' or 'vpnsvc', not 'root'. Output of 'root' indicates root_or_system level.

how_to_obtain.instruction: On Linux, check the systemd unit file for the User= directive to confirm the configured service account.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: User= is set to a dedicated non-root, non-sudo account. Empty User= means the service inherits root, which is root_or_system level.

how_to_obtain.instruction: On Windows, open Services (services.msc), locate the VPN service (e.g., Cisco AnyConnect VPN Agent, Juniper Network Connect), right-click > Properties > Log On tab. Review the account name. Then verify group membership in Computer Management > Local Users and Groups.
how_to_obtain.navigation: Windows: services.msc > [VPN Service] > Properties > Log On tab | Computer Management > Local Users and Groups
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Log On As account is a dedicated service account, not LocalSystem, Local Service with admin group membership, or a domain admin account.

how_to_obtain.instruction: On Windows, use sc.exe to query the service configuration and determine the account name, then check group membership.
how_to_obtain.command: sc qc "Cisco AnyConnect VPN Agent" && net user %SERVICE_ACCOUNT% /domain 2>nul || net localgroup administrators
how_to_obtain.expected_output: SERVICE_START_NAME reflects a least-privilege account that is not a member of Administrators, Domain Admins, or equivalent groups.

option_description: Indicates whether the OS account used to run the VPN service process is also referenced by other services, scheduled tasks, cron jobs, or application configurations, meaning compromise of the account from one vector exposes all consuming services simultaneously.
security_impact: The Rego policy triggers 'privileged_account_used_for_vpn_service_identity' when vpn_service_account_privilege_level is local_admin AND service_account_is_shared is true. A shared service account dramatically expands lateral movement risk: compromising the VPN service (a high-value internet-exposed target) also grants access to every other system and service using the same credential. Attackers can harvest the credential from any one consumer and pivot broadly without needing additional escalation techniques.

how_to_obtain.instruction: On Linux, identify the VPN service account name, then search for references to that account in other service unit files, cron entries, and application configuration files.
how_to_obtain.command: VPN_USER=$(systemctl show openvpn@server.service --property=User | cut -d= -f2); grep -rn "$VPN_USER" /etc/systemd/system/ /etc/cron* /etc/cron.d/ /opt/ /etc/*.conf 2>/dev/null | grep -v '#'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Only VPN-related unit files reference the account. References in other service files or application configs indicate the account is shared.

how_to_obtain.instruction: On Linux, check /etc/passwd for the service account's shell and home directory, then review .ssh/authorized_keys and any sudo rules that reference the account.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: The account has a non-login shell (e.g., /usr/sbin/nologin), no SSH authorized keys, and no sudo privileges beyond what is strictly required for the VPN service.

how_to_obtain.instruction: In Active Directory Users and Computers (for domain accounts), locate the service account, right-click > Properties > check the 'Member Of' tab for group memberships, then use 'Find Objects' or a PowerShell query to enumerate other services referencing the same account across domain-joined hosts.
how_to_obtain.navigation: Active Directory Users and Computers > [Service Account] > Properties > Member Of | Attribute Editor > servicePrincipalName
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Service principal names (SPNs) should be limited to VPN-related entries only; multiple SPNs or group memberships covering non-VPN services indicate a shared account.

how_to_obtain.instruction: On Windows, query the Service Control Manager for all services using the VPN service account to detect sharing.
how_to_obtain.command: Get-WmiObject Win32_Service | Where-Object {$_.StartName -like '*vpnsvc*' -or $_.StartName -like '*vpn_svc*'} | Select-Object Name, StartName, State
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Only VPN-related services (e.g., Cisco AnyConnect VPN Agent) appear in the results. Multiple service names indicate account sharing.

option_description: Indicates whether pre-shared keys (PSKs), private key passphrases, or service account credentials are stored in unencrypted plaintext within VPN gateway configuration files on disk, rather than being stored as references to an external secrets manager or in an encrypted vault.
security_impact: The Rego policy triggers 'hardcoded_secrets_in_configuration_files' when plaintext_secrets_detected is true and either secrets_manager_integrated is false or the config file permissions are world-readable or group-readable by unintended principals. Plaintext secrets in config files are directly exploitable as credentials stored in files (T1552.001) and private key theft (T1552.004). Any user or process with file read access—including malware with limited privileges—can extract PSKs, enabling unauthorized tunnel establishment or service account impersonation.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Grep VPN configuration files for common plaintext secret patterns including PSK, passphrase, password, and secret keywords. Run as root to access restricted files.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: No output indicates no plaintext secrets are present. Any output lines containing literal key material (not variable references or secrets manager tokens) confirm plaintext secrets are detected.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Directly inspect /etc/ipsec.secrets (strongSwan/libreswan) for RSA private key passphrases and PSK entries, and /etc/openvpn/*.conf for inline <tls-auth>, <cert>, or <key> blocks containing embedded key material.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: PSK entries in ipsec.secrets should be absent or replaced with certificate references (%cert). OpenVPN configs should reference external file paths rather than containing inline PEM blocks.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Check file permissions on VPN configuration files to assess exposure surface even if secrets are present; world-readable files with secrets are the highest risk combination.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Permissions on secret-bearing files should be 600 or 640, owned by root or the VPN service account. World-readable permissions (o+r) or group-readable by non-VPN groups indicate elevated exposure.

how_to_obtain.instruction: For commercial appliances (Cisco ASA, FortiGate, Palo Alto): export the running configuration from the management GUI and open in a text editor. Search for PSK, preshared-key, passphrase, password, and secret tokens. Verify that sensitive values are masked as '****' or reference a key vault integration rather than appearing as cleartext strings.
how_to_obtain.navigation: Cisco ASA: Tools > Backup Configurations | FortiGate: System > Config > Backup | Palo Alto: Device > Setup > Operations > Export Named Configuration Snapshot
how_to_obtain.expected_output: All credential and key fields are either masked (displayed as '****' in GUI) or reference an external vault/HSM identifier. Any cleartext credential value visible in the exported config confirms plaintext_secrets_detected = true.

option_description: Controls whether the VPN gateway retrieves sensitive credentials (pre-shared keys, service account passwords, certificate passphrases) from a dedicated secrets management platform such as HashiCorp Vault, AWS Secrets Manager, or Azure Key Vault, rather than reading plaintext values directly from local configuration files on disk.
security_impact: The Rego policy flags hardcoded_secrets_in_configuration_files when plaintext_secrets_detected is true and secrets_manager_integrated is false. Without secrets manager integration, any attacker or unauthorized local user with filesystem access can extract PSKs, private key passphrases, or service credentials directly from config files. This maps to MITRE T1552.001 (Credentials in Files) and T1552.004 (Private Keys). Enabling secrets manager integration removes the static secret from disk entirely, replacing it with a runtime API call to a controlled, audited vault.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Inspect the primary VPN daemon configuration file for secret reference syntax versus inline plaintext values. Look for patterns indicating vault agent socket paths, AWS Secrets Manager ARN references, or environment variable injection rather than literal credential strings.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Secret fields should reference a path such as 'vault:secret/vpn/psk' or an environment variable like '${VPN_PSK}' rather than a plaintext string like 'MySecretKey123'.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Search VPN configuration files for common secret field names and check whether values look like plaintext credentials or external references. Grep recursively across the VPN config directory.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: No output indicates no plaintext inline secrets. Any match showing a literal string value is a finding.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Review the VPN gateway startup scripts and service unit files to confirm whether a secrets manager agent (e.g., Vault Agent, AWS SSM Parameter Store fetch script, Azure Key Vault reference) is invoked prior to or during service startup to inject secrets at runtime.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Service unit or init script should show a pre-start hook calling vault agent, aws secretsmanager get-secret-value, or az keyvault secret show before the VPN daemon launches.

how_to_obtain.instruction: If the VPN gateway is cloud-hosted (e.g., AWS Client VPN, Azure VPN Gateway), query the cloud provider API to verify that secret references in the gateway configuration point to managed secret ARNs or Key Vault URIs rather than inline values.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Authentication options should reference certificate ARNs or directory service IDs managed through AWS Certificate Manager or Secrets Manager, not embedded credential strings.

typical_values: false (common in legacy on-premises deployments where PSKs are stored directly in ipsec.conf or vpnd.conf)
true (expected in cloud-native or modern deployments using Vault Agent sidecar or cloud-native secrets references)

option_description: Records the octal filesystem permission mode assigned to VPN configuration files that contain or reference sensitive credentials. This attribute captures how restrictively the operating system controls read and write access to these files, determining which OS users and processes can inspect or modify VPN secrets.
security_impact: The Rego policy evaluates hardcoded_secrets_in_configuration_files and checks config_file_permission_mode against a regex that matches any mode granting read access to group or world (e.g., 644, 640, 664, 604). When plaintext_secrets_detected is true and the permission mode allows group or world read, the exposure is flagged regardless of whether a secrets manager is used. This directly enables T1552.001 (Credentials in Files) since any process or user in the file-owning group, or any local user on a world-readable file, can cat the config and extract PSKs or passphrases. The secure baseline is 600 (owner read/write only) or 400 (owner read-only) so only the VPN daemon process running as its designated service account can access the file.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Use stat to retrieve the octal permission mode of the primary VPN configuration files. Run this for each relevant config file including IPsec secrets files and OpenVPN config files.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Each line shows the octal mode followed by the filename, e.g., '600 /etc/ipsec.secrets'. Values of 640 or 644 are findings; 600 or 400 are acceptable.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Use ls -l to obtain symbolic permission notation and owner/group information for all VPN configuration files, confirming that group and other permission bits are clear for sensitive files.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Permission string should begin with '-rw-------' (600) or '-r--------' (400). Strings showing '-rw-r--r--' (644) or '-rw-r-----' (640) are findings.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Recursively find all VPN-related configuration files with permissions more permissive than 600 to identify any files that grant group or world read access.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: No output means all sensitive files are restricted to 600 or 400. Any file listed is a finding requiring permission tightening.

typical_values: 600 (secure baseline; owner read/write only, no group or world access)
640 (common misconfiguration; grants group read access, allowing any member of the VPN group to read secrets)
644 (insecure default on some distributions; world-readable, any local user can extract secrets)
400 (hardened read-only; acceptable when the daemon runs as the owning user)

option_description: Determines whether the VPN gateway enforces an account lockout mechanism that temporarily disables or locks a user account after a defined number of consecutive failed authentication attempts. This control applies to the VPN authentication layer regardless of whether the backend is a local user database, RADIUS server, LDAP directory, or built-in identity provider.
security_impact: The Rego policy triggers no_account_lockout_or_rate_limiting_on_authentication when both account_lockout_enabled and rate_limiting_enabled are false, directly exposing the gateway to T1110.001 (Password Guessing), T1110.003 (Password Spraying), and T1110.004 (Credential Stuffing). Without lockout, an attacker can attempt unlimited authentication requests against any user account. A secondary Rego condition also flags the exposure when account_lockout_enabled is true but max_failed_auth_attempts exceeds 100 and rate_limiting_enabled is also absent, meaning a nominally enabled lockout with an excessively high threshold provides no effective protection.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Inspect the VPN gateway authentication configuration section for lockout-related directives. On StrongSwan or Libreswan, check for PAM integration with pam_faillock or pam_tally2. On OpenVPN Access Server, review the as.conf or node.conf for lockout settings.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Presence of a directive such as 'cs.max_login_failures=5' or 'auth.lockout.enable=true' indicates lockout is configured. Absence or a value of 0 indicates no lockout.

how_to_obtain.instruction: On Linux-based VPN gateways using PAM for authentication, check the PAM configuration for the VPN service to confirm pam_faillock or pam_tally2 is present and configured with a deny threshold.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Output should show lines such as 'auth required pam_faillock.so deny=5 unlock_time=900'. No output or absence of deny parameter indicates lockout is not enforced.

how_to_obtain.instruction: For commercial VPN solutions (Cisco ASA/FTD, Palo Alto GlobalProtect, Fortinet FortiGate), navigate to the authentication or AAA policy section in the management console and locate the account lockout or failed login threshold setting.
how_to_obtain.navigation: Cisco ASDM: Configuration > Remote Access VPN > AAA/Local Users > Account Lockout | FortiGate: VPN > SSL-VPN Settings > Authentication/Portal > Lockout Settings | Palo Alto: Device > Authentication Profile > Lockout tab
how_to_obtain.expected_output: A lockout policy is enabled with a maximum attempts value between 3 and 10, and a lockout duration of at least 5 minutes.

how_to_obtain.instruction: If authentication is delegated to a RADIUS or LDAP server, interview the identity team to confirm whether the backend directory (Active Directory, FreeRADIUS) enforces account lockout for VPN-sourced authentication requests and verify that lockout events propagate back to the VPN gateway.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Documented policy showing AD Fine-Grained Password Policy or Default Domain Policy has account lockout threshold set, and RADIUS NPS is configured to enforce these policies for VPN authentication requests.

typical_values: false (common on legacy IPsec gateways with local user databases and no PAM integration)
true (expected when PAM pam_faillock is configured or when a commercial gateway has lockout policy enabled)

option_description: Controls whether the VPN gateway enforces throttling or rate limiting on authentication attempts originating from a given source IP address or targeting a specific user account. This mechanism introduces delay penalties, connection attempt caps per time window, or automated blocking of high-frequency authentication sources without requiring a full account lockout.
security_impact: The Rego policy flags no_account_lockout_or_rate_limiting_on_authentication when neither account_lockout_enabled nor rate_limiting_enabled is true. Rate limiting is particularly important as a complementary or standalone control because account lockout can be weaponized for denial-of-service against legitimate users, whereas source-IP-based rate limiting disrupts password spray and credential stuffing campaigns (T1110.003, T1110.004) without locking valid accounts. Rate limiting also addresses distributed attacks where a single account lockout threshold is not reached per account but many accounts are targeted sequentially.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Check whether fail2ban or a similar host-based intrusion prevention tool is installed, active, and has a jail configured for the VPN authentication service to block source IPs after repeated failures.
how_to_obtain.command: fail2ban-client status 2>/dev/null && fail2ban-client status vpn 2>/dev/null || fail2ban-client status openvpn 2>/dev/null
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Output should show an active jail named 'vpn', 'openvpn', or 'ipsec' with a non-zero maxretry value and a bantime. 'No such jail' indicates rate limiting via fail2ban is not configured.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Inspect fail2ban jail configuration files or the VPN daemon's built-in rate limiting directives to confirm a connection rate limit is applied to the authentication endpoint.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: File should contain '[openvpn]' or '[vpn]' section with 'enabled = true', 'maxretry = 5', and 'findtime = 300' or similar values. File absence or 'enabled = false' is a finding.

how_to_obtain.instruction: For commercial VPN platforms, navigate to the threat prevention or DoS protection settings to verify per-source authentication rate limiting is configured and applied to the remote access VPN authentication listener port.
how_to_obtain.navigation: Palo Alto NGFW: Network > Network Profiles > Zone Protection > Reconnaissance Protection | Fortinet FortiGate: Policy & Objects > DoS Policy > Authentication Rate Limit | Cisco FTD: Policies > Access Control > Prefilter > Rate-Based Attack Prevention
how_to_obtain.expected_output: A rate-based policy exists targeting the VPN authentication port (TCP/443 or UDP/500/4500) with a per-source connection rate limit configured and action set to block or drop.

how_to_obtain.instruction: On Linux-based gateways, verify whether iptables or nftables rules implementing connection rate limiting are applied to the VPN authentication service port, restricting new connection attempts per source IP per time interval.
how_to_obtain.command: iptables -L INPUT -n -v 2>/dev/null | grep -E '(limit|recent|connlimit)' || nft list ruleset 2>/dev/null | grep -E '(limit rate|ct count)'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Output should show rules such as '-m limit --limit 5/min' or '-m connlimit --connlimit-above 10' applied to the VPN port. No matching rules indicate rate limiting is not enforced at the network layer.

typical_values: false (common on self-managed OpenVPN or StrongSwan deployments without an explicit fail2ban or firewall rate-limiting rule)
true (expected on commercial gateways with built-in DoS protection or Linux gateways with fail2ban and iptables rate limiting configured)

option_description: Specifies the numeric threshold of consecutive failed authentication attempts that triggers the account lockout or rate-limiting enforcement action. A value of 0 indicates no limit is configured, meaning the lockout or rate-limiting feature is either disabled or has no effective threshold. Values between 1 and 9999 represent the configured attempt ceiling before the protective action fires.
security_impact: The Rego policy references this attribute in no_account_lockout_or_rate_limiting_on_authentication with the condition that if account_lockout_enabled is true but max_failed_auth_attempts exceeds 100 and rate_limiting_enabled is also false, the exposure is still flagged. This recognizes that a lockout threshold of 101 or higher provides essentially no protection against automated brute-force or password-spray tooling, which can trivially stay under such a high ceiling while systematically testing password lists. Industry best practice establishes the secure threshold at 5 or fewer consecutive failures. A value of 0 always results in an exposure finding as it signals the lockout feature is unconfigured.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Read the configured maximum failed attempts value directly from the VPN gateway authentication configuration file or the associated PAM configuration for the VPN service.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: The file should contain a line such as 'deny = 5' specifying the maximum consecutive failures. Absence of the deny directive or a value of 0 is a finding.

how_to_obtain.instruction: On OpenVPN Access Server, query the configuration database for the maximum login failures setting, which maps directly to this attribute.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Output should include a key-value pair such as 'cs.max_login_failures: 5'. A value of 0 or absence of the key indicates no lockout threshold is set.

how_to_obtain.instruction: On StrongSwan or Libreswan with PAM authentication, extract the deny parameter from the pam_faillock or pam_tally2 configuration lines in the PAM stack for the VPN service.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Output should show 'deny=5' or a similarly low value. Values of 'deny=0', values above 10, or no output are findings requiring remediation.

how_to_obtain.instruction: For Cisco ASA/FTD, Palo Alto GlobalProtect, or Fortinet FortiGate, locate the account lockout threshold setting in the authentication policy configuration panel and record the numeric value shown.
how_to_obtain.navigation: Cisco ASDM: Configuration > Device Management > Users/AAA > AAA Servers > Lockout Policy > Max Failures | FortiGate GUI: VPN > SSL-VPN Settings > Lockout Duration and Attempt fields | Palo Alto: Device > Authentication Profile > [Profile Name] > Lockout tab > Failed Attempts field
how_to_obtain.expected_output: The 'Maximum Failed Attempts' or equivalent field should display a value between 3 and 5. A value of 0, blank, or greater than 10 is a finding.

typical_values: 0 (default on many unconfigured gateways; indicates no lockout threshold and is always a finding)
3 (hardened configuration; common in high-security or compliance-driven environments)
5 (industry best practice baseline; recommended by CIS benchmarks and NIST SP 800-63B guidance)
10 (permissive but still functional; provides some brute-force resistance but below best practice)
100 or higher (effectively disabled; found on legacy systems where lockout was nominally enabled but threshold never tuned)
